newsitem.title: CANADA: Bank of Canada head bullish on economy, dollar.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Canada head bullish on economy, dollar.

text.p: Bank of Canada Gov. Gordon Thiessen said on Wednesday the Canadian economy and dollar appeared set for strong gains in the next few years.
But the head of Canada's central bank added that the country needed to maintain confidence in its currency and could not operate a completely "made-in-Canada" interest rate policy.
The made-in-Canada policy refers to the Bank of Canada's recent moves to set interest rates independent of the U.S. Federal Reserve.

"The made-in-Canada monetary policy does not mean completely independent interest rates. Interest rates are always going to be affected by what goes on in the rest of the world," Thiessen told a news conference after a speech in this east coast city.
Thiessen told a Halifax business group that last year's sharp decline in interest rates was reflected in stronger economic growth and domestic spending.
But he said that inflation did not appear to be a threat because there was still a lot of slack in the Canadian economy.

Last year, the Bank of Canada cut interest rates 11 times, bringing the key bank rate, similar to the U.S. federal funds rates, to its lowest level since 1961. Canada's bank rate is now at 3.25 percent, compared with the U.S. fed funds rate at 5.5 percent. The federal funds rate is the rate banks charge each other for short term loans.

But the growing divide between Canadian and U.S. short-term rates has hurt the Canadian dollar, as higher U.S. rates attract capital away from Canada. The Canadian dollar recently weakened to a two-year low, which prompted some economists to call for a Bank of Canada rate hike.
Thiessen told reporters after his speech that Canada's positive fundamentals, such as inflation lower than that of the United States, pointed to an upward trend for the currency.
Some of the recent weakness in the Canadian dollar was likely to disappear as the Canadian economy moved toward full capacity, he said.
